subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
subtype: Approach: decide to stay with a set review and adjust [Revision]
passage:
After two months on the new team, Arohi sat at her desk with a blank sheet and asked herself whether the job had earned more time. The work was better than before. She had learnt two tools, and mornings no longer felt heavy. She decided to stay.

But she wanted the staying to mean something. She wrote it down: by the end of six months, lead one small project, learn a reporting tool, and earn an increase that matches the extra work. Then she went to Rekha, her manager, and asked for a review on the fifteenth of March to see how it was going.

At home she kept an updated CV in a folder, just in case the goals were missed. It was there if she needed it, and she hoped she wouldn't.

qa.q: On what date did Arohi ask for a review?
qa.a: On the fifteenth of March.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel about the job after two months on the new team?
qa.a: Arohi felt more hopeful and engaged, since the work was better and mornings no longer felt heavy.

qa.q: What could Arohi do if Rekha said the goals were unrealistic, and why?
qa.a: Arohi could ask which goals are realistic and agree a revised set in writing, because a review works only if both sides accept the targets.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Arohi's request for a review date?
qa.a: Rekha may see a staff member who takes the job seriously and wants clear feedback, which makes it easier to plan growth for Arohi.

grounding: After a trial, the person stays for six more months with a written goal for skills and pay, a scheduled review and the exit plan kept ready.

subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
subtype: Approach: ask what would change the decision [Thinking]
passage:
The other company's offer would expire on Friday, and it was already Wednesday. Jagdish sat at the kitchen table with his sister Arohi, who kept refilling his tea. "Every hour I go back and forth," he said. "I need something firmer than a feeling."

He took a page and wrote: I will stay only if I see three things. One: a clear path to a senior role within a year. Two: a move to the platform team. Three: a manager who gives feedback each month. Then he underlined the last line: Can any of these happen?

On Thursday he asked his manager about each condition in plain words. Two seemed possible; one did not. That was enough to calm his mind before Friday.

qa.q: What did Jagdish's sister do while he was writing?
qa.a: She kept refilling his tea.

qa.q: What is Jagdish feeling at the kitchen table with the deadline so near?
qa.a: Jagdish feels pressed and unsettled, going back and forth every hour and wanting something firmer than a feeling.

qa.q: What could Jagdish do if his manager cannot say for certain what will happen, and why?
qa.a: Jagdish could ask for the answers in writing by Friday morning or weigh the uncertainty in the decision, because the choice needs facts, not vague reassurance.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Jagdish's list of conditions?
qa.a: Arohi may feel relieved that her brother is turning a churning worry into questions that can be answered, and may be glad she could sit with him.

grounding: The person writes three conditions under which staying makes sense and checks whether they can happen before the deadline.

subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
subtype: Approach: switch to a lighter plan when burned out [Revision]
passage:
In Berlin, Ivan's evenings had blurred into one long sprint: work until seven, then a side project until midnight, then bed at one. By October he was forgetting simple words and snapping at his flatmate. He caught himself staring at an unfinished email for twenty minutes.

He walked into Fatima's office, his manager, and said honestly, "I think I'm burnt out." She did not argue. Together they planned two weeks of leave. Ivan also decided to pause the side project, which felt like relief and like loss at the same time.

During the break he slept, cooked, and walked by the river. Only afterwards did he open the question of whether to stay or move on. It looked different, and quieter, than it had in October.

qa.q: How long was the leave that Ivan and Fatima planned?
qa.a: Two weeks of leave.

qa.q: What was Ivan feeling about pausing the side project?
qa.a: Ivan felt relief and loss together, wanting the rest but sad about letting something he cared about wait.

qa.q: What could Ivan do when he returns to keep from burning out again, and why?
qa.a: Ivan could set a fixed end time for work and keep an evening free, because rest built into the week protects against another slide.

qa.q: How might Fatima see Ivan's coming to her office?
qa.a: Fatima may be worried yet appreciative that Ivan spoke up honestly, since it let them plan the leave rather than deal with a crisis.

grounding: Facing burnout, the person takes planned leave, drops a side project and revisits the decision after rest.

subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: list all demands and rank them by urgency and importance [Thinking]
passage:
Come, sit, Rafiq. When I was in my last year, my father fell ill, and as his only son I felt pulled in six directions. I'm Bhupen, and my first thought was to try to do everything. Then my roommate Kishan said, "Write all of it down."

So I did. Hospital visits, my exams, two assignments, cooking, the electricity bill. Beside each one I wrote two things: how urgent, how important. When I looked at it, two items were both urgent and important: my father's hospital appointments and the exam ahead. The rest could wait, be shared, or be dropped.

I told the lecturer I'd hand in the assignments late. I asked a cousin to sort out the bills. It felt awkward, but for the first time my head cleared.

qa.q: Whom did Bhupen tell about the late assignments?
qa.a: The lecturer.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel before he wrote the list?
qa.a: Bhupen felt overwhelmed, pulled in six directions and at first tempted to try to do everything.

qa.q: What choice at the list stage kept Bhupen from breaking down, and what else could he have done?
qa.a: Ranking everything by urgency and importance let him say no to the rest; he could also have asked Kishan or the cousin to take a larger share.

qa.q: How does Kishan see Bhupen's situation in the story?
qa.a: Kishan saw a roommate heading for exhaustion and gave a practical nudge to write it down, which shows care.

grounding: A final-year student lists hospital visits, exams, assignments and household tasks, and ranks treatment appointments and the exam as top priorities.

subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: share the care schedule with siblings and relatives [Action]
passage:
Day 1. Vaibhav spread a large sheet on the dining table and drew a grid of seven days. Hospital stays, medicine pickups and cooking, each in a colour. Mum's care had been falling on him alone for weeks, and his eyes were sore from studying at night.

Day 4. He phoned his brother Jomon, his Masi and a neighbour. Jomon took Monday and Thursday nights at the hospital, Masi took Tuesday's cooking, and the neighbour offered to collect medicines on Saturdays. Vaibhav wrote each name in its slot.

Day 18. The rota had been followed for two weeks. He sat his exam with his mind clear and slept properly the night before. Mum said to him, softly, "You look better, beta."

qa.q: Which nights did Jomon take at the hospital?
qa.a: Monday and Thursday nights.

qa.q: How was Vaibhav feeling before he made the rota?
qa.a: Vaibhav was worn out and strained, shown by the sore eyes and the weeks of care falling on him alone.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav add to the rota to keep it working, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could set a fixed time each week to check that everyone is comfortable with their slots, because a shared plan needs small adjustments as things change.

qa.q: How might Mum see the new rota?
qa.a: Mum likely feels comforted that the family is sharing the care and relieved that Vaibhav is resting, as her remark on his looking better suggests.

grounding: The student writes a weekly rota and asks a sibling, an aunt and a neighbour to take fixed slots, sharing the care.

subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: take on everything alone to prove devotion [Pitfall]
passage:
Charu got up at four each morning in the village near Nashik: milk the buffalo, cook, wash Bapu's clothes, since he could no longer leave his bed, then catch the seven o'clock bus to college. At night she sat by his bed, on the mat, and studied by the lamp. She slept four hours, and told herself that asking for help would mean she didn't love him enough.

Sangeeta from the next house came by twice with rotis and said, "Let me sit with him tonight." Charu smiled and refused both times.

By the third week she failed the practical test. Then she snapped at Bapu when he asked for water, and saw his face fall. She sat outside on the step, and realised that being exhausted had made her worse at caring.

qa.q: Where did Charu study at night?
qa.a: By the lamp, sitting on the mat beside Bapu's bed.

qa.q: Why did Charu refuse Sangeeta's offers?
qa.a: Charu felt that asking for help would mean not loving Bapu enough, so she saw accepting as disloyalty.

qa.q: What could Charu do now, and why?
qa.a: Charu could accept Sangeeta's offer for a night or two and use the time to sleep, because rest makes her both a better student and a better carer.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel after being turned away twice?
qa.a: Sangeeta may feel concerned and a little helpless, seeing Charu tired but not knowing how to help someone who will not accept it.

grounding: Feeling that asking for help is disloyal, the student does every task and sleeps four hours, leading to a failed test and short temper.

subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: talk to teachers about accommodations [Action]
passage:
I'll tell you what worked for me, beta. When I was twenty-one, my mother had a long illness, and I was drowning in missed lectures. I'm Santosh. I was scared to speak to anyone at the department, because I didn't want to look like someone making excuses.

But one Monday I knocked on Professor Sabina's door. She was the head. I told her plainly what was happening at home, said I'd miss some classes, and asked two things: a little flexibility on deadlines, and a way to get the class notes online.

She listened, then said, "Why didn't you come sooner?" She gave me two extra weeks on one paper and arranged for a classmate to share the notes. It cost me an awkward ten minutes. Not asking would have cost much more.

qa.q: Whose door did Santosh knock on that Monday?
qa.a: Professor Sabina's door.

qa.q: Why was Santosh reluctant to speak to anyone at the department?
qa.a: Santosh was afraid of looking like someone making excuses, so pride and embarrassment held the request back.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Santosh's semester, and what could have happened otherwise?
qa.a: Knocking on the door and asking plainly changed things; without it, missed lectures and deadlines would probably have piled up unnoticed.

qa.q: How does Professor Sabina see the request when Santosh finally comes?
qa.a: Professor Sabina listens without judgement, and asking why Santosh did not come sooner suggests she would gladly have helped earlier.

grounding: The student explains the situation to the department head and asks for deadline flexibility and class notes online.

subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: contingency plan for a hospital emergency [Thinking]
passage:
Charu: I made a folder in case Papa's condition worsens
Siddharth: What's in it?
Charu: All prescriptions, every report in date order, the insurance papers, and a page with Dr Rao's number and the hospital's front desk
Siddharth: Good. And if it happens at night?
Charu: That's the second part. I asked Masi and Chacha yesterday. If it gets serious, Masi stays at home with Mummy and you and I go to the hospital. Chacha books the tickets
Siddharth: So no one is scrambling
Charu: Exactly. The folder lives in the blue bag by the door, and I told everyone where it is
Siddharth: I'll take a photo of every page too

qa.q: Where does the folder live?
qa.a: In the blue bag by the door.

qa.q: How does Charu seem to feel about preparing the folder?
qa.a: Charu seems anxious about what could happen but steadier for having a plan, since preparing gives a sense of control.

qa.q: What could Charu and Siddharth add to the plan, and why?
qa.a: They could save the doctor's number in their phones and check the papers every month, because a plan only helps if it stays current.

qa.q: How might Masi feel about being given the job of staying with Mummy?
qa.a: Masi probably feels trusted and responsible, and glad to know the role in advance instead of being caught off guard.

grounding: The student prepares a folder of papers, saves the doctor's number and agrees with relatives on who travels if the condition worsens.

subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: study in small blocks around the caregiving day [Action]
passage:
Vasudha's revision time was scattered like torn paper, so she stopped waiting for the perfect hour. She wrote short notes on index cards, one idea on each, and slipped them into her bag.

On the bus to the taluka hospital she read three cards. In the waiting hall while Aai had her check-up, she asked her brother Jagdish to quiz her from the deck, and he held the cards like a game-show host. Between calls of the queue number she solved two problems in her notebook.

At night, after Aai slept, she kept one fixed hour for the hard topics, with tea and a clear table. By the end of the month, the cards had gone soft at the corners and her test paper came back with a good mark.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha ask Jagdish to quiz her?
qa.a: In the waiting hall, while Aai had her check-up.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel about her scattered time, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Vasudha felt frustrated but resourceful, as she stopped waiting for the perfect hour and started using every gap.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do if the night hour got cancelled, and why?
qa.a: Vasudha could move the hard topics to the first spare stretch the next day, because the routine holds as long as the hard work has a protected slot.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see quizzing Vasudha in the waiting hall?
qa.a: Jagdish probably enjoys being useful and turning a long, dull wait into a game, and may feel proud when her marks improve.

grounding: The student uses waiting hours and bus rides for short-note revision and keeps one fixed night hour for hard topics.

subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: notice signs of caregiver fatigue and step back [Revision]
passage:
Tanvir hadn't slept properly for three weeks. In the noisy ward, with one week left before the exam, he snapped at a nurse over a small thing, then apologised too many times. On the bus he realised he had been irritable every single day, and that the bad sleep never lifted.

He thought about it that evening. It isn't one bad day. It's the whole pattern. He called his Dilnaz khala and said, "I can't keep doing every night. Could you take two of them?" She said yes before he finished.

The next morning he booked a counselling session at the college. It was hard to admit, but the care he gave Dad had been getting sharper, and that was the real signal.

qa.q: How many nights did Tanvir ask Dilnaz khala to take?
qa.a: Two of them.

qa.q: How was Tanvir feeling as he snapped at the nurse and then apologised too many times?
qa.a: Tanvir was exhausted and ashamed, and the constant irritation and poor sleep made him see that he was worn out.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do on the nights off, and why?
qa.a: Tanvir could sleep and revise in a quiet place away from the ward, because rest helps both his exam and his patience when he returns.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz khala feel about being asked?
qa.a: Dilnaz khala said yes before Tanvir finished, so she probably felt glad to be asked and was worried he had carried so much alone.

grounding: Realising that irritation and poor sleep are constant, the student asks an aunt to take two nights and books a counselling session.
